Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
Let (M, d) be a metric space, and let (F_n) be a sequence of nonempty closed subsets with F_{n+1} ⊂ F_n and diam F_n → 0 as n → ∞.

We show that (M, d) is complete if and only if ∩_{n=1}^{∞} F_n ≠ ∅ for every such sequence.

For the forward direction, assume (M, d) is complete. Given x_n ∈ F_n for each n, is (x_n) a Cauchy sequence? Since F_{n+1} ⊂ F_n, any two points in F_n lie at distance at most diam F_n, which vanishes as n → ∞, so for m > n we have d(x_m, x_n) ≤ diam F_n → 0. Completeness of M therefore guarantees x = lim x_n ∈ M for any choice x_n ∈ F_n. Does x lie in F_k for every fixed k? Because F_k is closed and contains x_n for all n ≥ k (as F_n ⊂ F_k for n ≥ k), the limit x belongs to F_k for every k. Thus x ∈ ∩_{k=1}^{∞} F_k, confirming the intersection is nonempty.

For the converse, let (x_n) be an arbitrary Cauchy sequence in M. Define F_n = \overline{\{x_n, x_{n+1}, x_{n+2}, \ldots\}}, which is nonempty, closed, and satisfies F_{n+1} ⊂ F_n. Does diam F_n → 0? Since (x_n) is Cauchy, for every ε > 0 there exists N with d(x_p, x_q) < ε for all p, q ≥ N, whence diam F_n ≤ ε for n ≥ N, so indeed diam F_n → 0. The assumed intersection property yields a point x ∈ ∩_{n=1}^{∞} F_n ⊂ M. Does x coincide with lim x_n? Since x ∈ F_k for every k and F_k = \overline{\{x_k, x_{k+1}, \ldots\}}, we have d(x, x_k) → 0, so x = lim x_n. Does the converse hold, i.e., does the intersection property force completeness? Every Cauchy sequence in M converges to a point of M, completing the equivalence. Is the original property thus equivalent to completeness? It is, by the two inclusions just demonstrated.
